subject: Architecture
title: Chinese Stone Arch Bridges
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Chinese Stone Arch Bridges.

hook.text: China's Anji Bridge was built in 605 AD and is the world's oldest open-spandrel stone arch bridge.

buildup.text: Its open spandrels — arched openings above the main arch — reduce weight and allow floodwater to pass.

discovery.text: Europe didn't build open-spandrel bridges until 800 years later. Li Chun's design was centuries ahead.

twist.text: The bridge has survived ten major floods, eight wars, and multiple earthquakes — for over 1,400 years.

climax.text: Chinese bridge builders exported their skills across Asia — Japan, Korea, and Vietnam adopted the techniques.

punchline.text: A bridge from the year 605. Still standing. Still used.

quiz.question: What innovation makes the Anji Bridge structurally advanced?
options: Iron reinforcement inside the stone arch
Open-spandrel arches that reduce weight and pass floodwater
A movable central section for boat traffic

details.summary: The Zhaozhou Bridge in China, built around 605 CE, is the world's oldest open-spandrel stone arch bridge and was 700 years ahead of similar European designs.
details.whyItMatters: The Zhaozhou Bridge proves that Chinese engineering was centuries ahead of Europe in bridge design. Its open-spandrel technique solved flooding and weight problems that European builders wouldn't address for another 700 years.
takeaways: Built around 605 CE — the oldest open-spandrel stone arch bridge
Open spandrels reduce weight and pass floodwater through
Its design preceded similar European innovations by 700 years

faq.question: What makes an open-spandrel bridge different?
faq.answer: Closed-spandrel bridges fill the area between the arch and roadway with solid material. Open-spandrel bridges use smaller arches or openings instead, dramatically reducing weight and allowing floodwater to pass through rather than building pressure against the structure.

faq.question: Is the Zhaozhou Bridge still standing?
faq.answer: Yes. After surviving over 1,400 years including floods, earthquakes, and wars, it was restored in 1956. The original arch and foundation remain intact. It still carries pedestrian traffic and is one of China's most celebrated historical engineering achievements.
